name: PT Citra Putra Realty Tbk

frontmatter.title: Citra Putra Realty: two hotels, a thin balance sheet and a price with no cash-flow anchor
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp1,739, a return of -40.8%. The hotels are real and the 2026 recovery is visible, but on its own cash flow the equity is worth Rp114 today and Rp128 in a year, while the price is 25.8 times the former. The target is the concentrated-ownership lens, not a forecast that the price meets value within the year.
thesis: FY2025 revenue fell by a third and the first half of 2026 recovered most of it, but the profit pool is small: an asset-heavy pair of hotels whose interest bill takes most of the operating profit the hotels earn.

On a discounted cash flow at the house cost of capital the equity is worth Rp172 a share; the EV/EBITDA check is lower and the P/E check higher, and we explain both gaps in the valuation section rather than average them away, so the distance to the Rp2,940 price is not a method artefact.

CLAY is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, where its ten largest holders account for 99.89% of the shares against a free float of 18.6%, so flow, not cash flow, sets the marginal price; the lens keeps only part of the premium over twelve months.

Governance is the risk that dominates the fundamentals: a one-day trading suspension and an exchange-ordered incidental public expose in response to a price run, no dividend record, and an unfunded hospital project competing for the same thin equity.
Even the bull case is a bet on the regime, not on the rooms: mirrored business shocks leave the fundamental value far below the price, and only a large retained premium gets the target near it.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results, the first full-year test of the revenue recovery and of the cost base
Exchange free-float transition deadline for names below the fifteen per cent minimum (CLAY is above it)
Deadline for feedback in the MSCI Standalone consultation for Indonesia
Targeted completion of the Royal Sukadana hospital on the company two-year guidance from November 2025

Next quarterly HSC list review (quarterly cycle from the 20 October 2026 announcement), which decides whether CLAY stays out of the IHSG

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Citra Putra Realty at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp1,739**, an expected total return of **-40.8%** from the last close of Rp2,940 [S0]. The target is not our estimate of what the hotels are worth: our probability-weighted fundamental value is Rp114 a share today and Rp128 in twelve months, both after a liquidity discount of 30.0% for a stock whose three-month average daily turnover is tiny relative to its market value [S0]. The target is the house lens for concentrated-ownership names applied to that value: the price stands at 25.8 times today's value, and the lens assumes that 35.0% of the log gap closes over the next twelve months, leaving the rest of the premium in place [S0]. The call is therefore two statements at once, and the reader should keep them separate: the business is worth a small fraction of the market price, and the probability-weighted twelve-month value is still far above the business value because the float is small and the controller does not need to sell.

The company owns and operates two hotels. The Stones Hotel in Legian, Bali has 308 rooms on a 22,850 square metre site with 54,317 square metres of building [S7/F1][S9/F14][S9/F15]. Clay Hotel in Menteng, Jakarta has 70 rooms and sits in the central business district [S7/F2]. Both sit under the OSO Group umbrella, and the two properties are the group's main revenue contributors [S7]. There is no third asset in operation: the growth story is the Royal Sukadana hospital in Pontianak, which management describes as the strategic project for 2026 and targets for completion in one and a half to two years, with no disclosed cost, funding plan or return [S7].

The financial record is a recovery off a low base, not a compounding franchise. FY2025 revenue was IDR142.0bn, down from IDR230.6bn in FY2024, and EBITDA was IDR24.8bn [S0]. Revenue for the nine months to September 2025 was IDR103.6bn and net profit was IDR3.3bn, against IDR10.8bn a year earlier [S7/F4][S7/F5][S7/F6]. The first half of 2026 was better: revenue on the pack's quarterly series was roughly sixty per cent above the same period of 2025, and the third quarter extended the recovery, which is why our FY2026E revenue is IDR209.4bn, a 47.5% increase and above the pack's last twelve months [S0]. The balance sheet is the constraint. The last balance sheet the company itself published in the documents we archived is the November 2025 public expose, which showed total assets of IDR552.0bn, liabilities of IDR542.1bn and equity of IDR9.9bn at 30 September 2025, down from IDR13.0bn at the end of 2024 [S7/F7][S7/F8][S7/F9][S7/F10]. That snapshot is now stale, and the trend has run the other way: on the data pack's latest balance sheet, at 30 September 2026, debt is below the FY2025 year-end figure of IDR309.5bn and equity is above IDR17.1bn, while cash is a little lower than the IDR37.2bn held at the FY2025 year-end - about one per cent lower, so the liquidity trend is flat rather than improving [S0]. So the thin-equity argument is measured on a balance sheet that has repaired through 2026, not on the September 2025 trough, and it still holds: interest expense of IDR17.3bn against operating profit of IDR24.8bn is the whole of the problem, and a company in that position is priced by its lenders before its shareholders [S0].

Our variant view is that the market is paying for the float, not for the rooms. On the cash flow the two hotels generate, a discounted free-cash-flow valuation at a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9% gives Rp172 a share [S0]. The peer-median EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp97 and the peer-median P/E gives a value above it, so the two bracket the DCF and the result is not an artefact of one method [S0]. The reverse DCF says the same thing from the other side: at today's price the market needs FY2027E revenue growth of 41.5%, against our 8.0% base rate - 33.5% above it - a trajectory the company has never delivered and which the arrival data do not support [S0][S10]. What the price does reflect is a share register in which the ten largest holders account for 99.89% of the shares and 18.6% is free-floating, a stock the exchange suspended for a day in November 2024 for unusual price movement and placed on the high-shareholding-concentration list [S2][S8][S12]. The two measures are not in conflict: the concentration figure is the exchange's cumulative top-ten test, which is what puts a name on the HSC list, not one owner's stake (the governance section sets out both measures).

What moves the value. First, the revenue recovery: our base case assumes FY2026 revenue grows 47.5% and then fades to single digits, and the whole equity value is sensitive to whether the second half of 2026 holds the first half's run-rate [S0]. Second, the balance sheet: interest expense was IDR17.3bn in FY2025 on IDR309.5bn of debt, against operating profit of IDR24.8bn, so the lenders take most of the profit the hotels make [S0]. Note what that does to our numbers: the rate enters the earnings and the return on equity, not the valuation, because the free cash flow is struck before interest and discounted at the weighted average cost of capital. A refinancing therefore moves the earnings line and the case for a rights issue, and only a rights issue itself would move the per-share value, by dilution. We describe that risk in the risks section and do not shock it: neither the size nor the price of any issue is disclosed [S0]. Third, the regime: the free float, the HSC reviews and the MSCI consultation decide whether the premium persists, and none of them is a fundamental variable [S13][S14]. The hospital is a fourth, unquantified variable: it is either a new earnings stream or a call on equity the company does not have, and the record contains no cost or funding detail [S7].

Indonesia's listed hotel owners are mostly small, single-destination companies with one or two
trophy assets, and their shares are often held by a family group that treats the listing as a
financing vehicle rather than as a source of outside capital discipline. In that setting the traded
price can diverge from the replacement cost and earnings power of the buildings for long periods,
and the arrival statistics of the destination matter less to the share price than the intentions of
the controlling shareholder.

PT Citra Putra Realty listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in January 2019. The IPO sold 520m new shares, or a fifth of the paid-up capital, at Rp180 a share [S3/F12][S3/F13]. The company describes itself as a hospitality business operating through three segments, rooms, food and beverage and other departments, and its two properties are The Stones Hotel in Legian, Bali and Clay Hotel in Menteng, Jakarta [S0]. Both are operated under the OSO Group umbrella, and management presents them as the group's two main revenue contributors [S7].

The Bali asset is the larger of the two. The Stones occupies a 22,850 square metre site with 54,317 square metres of building and 308 rooms, with restaurants, a gym, spa, meeting space, a ballroom, laundry and airport transfer [S9/F14][S9/F15][S7/F1]. The restaurants named in the company's own presentation are Stones Kitchen, Blue Safir and The Long Rice Stable [S9]. The Jakarta asset is a city hotel of 70 rooms on a much smaller footprint in Jalan Blora, Menteng, with a café, business centre, massage and laundry service [S7/F2][S9]. The mix matters for the earnings: the Bali hotel carries the resort rate and the seasonality, the Jakarta hotel carries the corporate and government demand that is more cyclical than the leisure demand.

The strategy disclosed at the 2025 public expose has two legs, and only one of them is a hotel strategy: optimise the operation of the two hotels to restore revenue, and continue building the Royal Sukadana hospital in Pontianak as the company's main development project, targeted for completion in one and a half to two years depending on construction [S7]. The company frames itself as a property developer and investor rather than a hotel operator, and the hospital is consistent with that: it is a property development with a healthcare tenant rather than a hotel the company would manage [S9]. No cost, funding plan, bed count or return has been disclosed for the hospital in the material we could archive, which is why we do not put a project value in the valuation bridge [S7].

Market position is small and local. The Stones competes in the Legian-Seminyak resort cluster against internationally branded five-star properties, and Clay Hotel competes in the Jakarta mid-scale city segment. Neither is a leader on any measure the company discloses, and the company does not publish occupancy, average room rate or revenue per available room [S7]. The group structure is the more important fact about the business: the company is a subsidiary of PT Citra Putra Mandiri and sits inside OSO Group, and the share register is highly concentrated [S0][S7]. The controlling shareholder is not disclosed in the data pack beyond the parent name, and the annual report that would name the ultimate beneficiary is not in our archive; we flag that as an evidence gap rather than fill it.

The workforce is small, consistent with an owner that outsources hotel management and keeps a thin corporate centre [S0]. That is efficient when the hotels are full and brutal when they are not, because there is little cost left to cut: FY2025 showed exactly that, with revenue down a third and the operating cost line cut almost in half to keep operating profit flat [S0].

The relevant market is Indonesian domestic and inbound travel, and specifically two destinations with different demand drivers. Bali is an international leisure market: BPS Bali recorded 4.5m foreign tourist arrivals in the first eight months of 2026, -1.6% against the same period of 2025 [S10/F16][S10/F17]. That is the single most important external number for The Stones, because a resort hotel's rate and occupancy move with the arrival curve and with the mix between Australian, Chinese, Indian and European source markets. Jakarta is a domestic corporate, government and MICE market, driven by office occupancy, conference calendars and the government budget cycle, and it is the more defensive of the two in a weak year and the less exciting in a strong one.

The industry's cost structure explains the earnings pattern. Hotel costs are largely fixed in the short run: rooms cost, staff, utilities and the property charge do not fall with occupancy, while the revenue line does. That is why FY2025 revenue fell by a third while operating profit barely moved: the company cut the cost base hard, and the FY2025 cost line is now low enough that the recovery flows through at a high incremental margin [S0]. It also means a second demand shock would hit the equity, not the cost base, because there is little left to cut.

Competitive positioning is weak but not hopeless. The Stones is a well-located Legian property with a large room count and full facilities, and its owner has kept it open and operating through the downturn [S7]. Its disadvantage is brand: it is an independent property competing against international chains with global distribution systems, loyalty programmes and management contracts that bring both rate discipline and demand. Clay Hotel's advantage is location and cost, and its disadvantage is that Jakarta's mid-scale segment has abundant supply. Neither asset has a moat in the sense the compounder card requires: there is no network effect, no switching cost, no distribution density and no evidence of brand pricing power. The moat question is therefore answered honestly: the durable advantage is the land, not the operation.

The five forces are unfavourable on four of five. Supplier power is low for consumables but high for the property itself, because the asset cannot move. Buyer power is high: leisure travellers and corporate bookers compare on price across a deep supply of rooms, and the online travel agencies capture part of the rate. New entrants are a real threat in Jakarta's mid-scale segment and a slow one in Legian, where land is scarce and permits are hard. Substitutes are abundant, from serviced apartments to villa rentals. Rivalry is high in both markets. The one favourable force is that the Bali land bank is a scarce asset with replacement value well above its book value, which is why the downside to the equity is bounded by the property rather than by the earnings [S9].

Regulation touches the name in three places. Hotel operations are licensed and taxed locally, with a regional hotel and restaurant tax on top of corporate income tax; the company's effective tax rate was already above the statutory rate in FY2025 because of non-deductible items [S0]. Capital markets regulation matters more: the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration regime, under which HSC names left the IHSG calculation in early November 2026 [S12], the free-float minimum raised to fifteen per cent with transition deadlines from March 2027, and the MSCI consultation on Indonesia's classification, opened in mid-October 2026 with feedback due by end-April 2027 and a decision by mid-2027 [S13][S14]. Those dates bear directly on the price of a stock like this. And the hospital project is a regulated healthcare development, with licensing and construction permits that the record does not describe [S7].

External influences are the rupiah, the Indonesian rate cycle and the destination cycle. The company earns rupiah and borrows rupiah, so it has no direct FX mismatch; the indirect channel is that a weaker rupiah makes Bali cheaper for foreign visitors, which helps arrivals, and raises the cost of any imported equipment for the hospital. The rate cycle matters through the debt: with IDR309.5bn of borrowings against IDR17.1bn of equity, every hundred basis points on the cost of debt is a large fraction of earnings [S0]. The macro desk's Indonesian rate path is therefore a direct earnings input for this name, not a background variable.

The historical record is short and volatile. Revenue was IDR224.6bn in FY2023 and IDR230.6bn in FY2024, then fell to IDR142.0bn in FY2025 [S0]. Gross margin went from 49.6% to 51.8% to 43.6% over the same years, and the operating cost line was cut from IDR89.0bn to IDR37.2bn, which is why operating profit held at IDR24.8bn even as revenue collapsed [S0]. Attributable profit was IDR4.9bn, and almost all of the operating profit went to the lenders: interest expense was IDR17.3bn [S0].

The revenue build for the forecast starts from the nine months already reported, not from a growth rate applied to FY2025. The pack carries three consecutive 2026 quarters that rose from the first to the third, and the nine-month total is already above the whole of FY2025 [S0]. Our FY2026E of IDR209.4bn, a 47.5% increase, is that nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter set at the prior year's own seasonal ratio: revenue in Q4 2025 was about three-quarters of the third quarter of 2025, and applying that ratio to the third quarter of 2026 implies a fourth quarter at the prior-year level plus roughly forty per cent, i.e. one that grows at the same year-on-year rate as the third quarter instead of collapsing [S0]. The bridge is deliberately visible, because a fourth quarter at only the prior-year level or below would be a large unsourced decline after three improving quarters. FY2026E revenue is also above the pack's last twelve months, which is the minimum consistency test for a forecast made on a growing quarterly series [S0]. We then fade growth to 8.0%, 6.0% and 5.0% before terminal growth of 3.0%: a two-asset operator with no room pipeline cannot compound faster than the destination, and the only growth asset it has disclosed, the hospital, has no numbers attached to it [S7]. On this path FY2027E revenue returns to about the FY2024 level, so the forecast recovers the pre-trough business and does not assume a new one.

Margins are the second decision, and they are taken from the same four quarters rather than rounded. On the four quarters to June 2026 the pack gives a gross margin of 54.6% and an all-in operating cost ratio of 25.6%, which is the observed 29.0% EBIT margin of those quarters; we hold both components and the margin follows [S0]. That gross margin is above FY2024's 51.8% and well above the FY2025 trough of 43.6%, and it is below the twelve months to September 2026, so the calibration sits inside the run-rate rather than above it [S0]. The trough is the outlier, we have no archived segment data showing a permanent mix shift toward lower-margin food and beverage, and the pack's quarterly cost lines are noisy enough that we will not extrapolate the strongest quarter either: a haircut below the four-quarter run-rate would be an unsourced caution and the best quarter would assume the recent mix holds [S0]. That produces an EBIT margin of 29.0% against 17.4% in FY2025: the step is the revenue recovery against a cost base already cut, not a new margin assumption, and it sits under the twelve-month EBIT margin the pack now shows [S0].

Depreciation is the one line we cannot take from the filing, and it is a LEVEL, not a share of revenue. The data pack reports D&A of IDR0.0bn against PP&E of IDR428.2bn, which cannot be the real charge and makes the pack's EBITDA equal to its EBIT [S0]. A building stock of that size depreciated over a thirty-year hotel life is roughly fifteen billion rupiah a year on the company's own disclosure of the Legian site and floor area [S9/F14][S9/F15]. The template applies a ratio to revenue, so the ratio falls as revenue grows: the ratio is 7.2% in FY2026E and declines to 5.7% by FY2030E, which holds the charge at about IDR15.1bn rather than letting an add-back rise on a shrinking asset base. EBIT is unaffected because the operating cost line is taken all-in; the EBITDA line and the free cash flow both depend on this level, and the FY2025 LK depreciation note is the one document that would confirm it.

Cash flow and the balance sheet are where the story turns. Reported operating cash flow was positive in FY2025 and capex was only IDR10.6bn, so the business did generate cash even in the trough [S0]. The engine's FY2025A free cash flow to the firm is IDR-73.5bn, and the difference is not operations but the working-capital line: the engine charges IDR79.5bn of working capital against the year, a swing driven by the move in the pack's balance-sheet working capital to IDR-65.1bn: deposits, related-party and tax balances that the reported direct-method cash-flow statement did not treat as an operating outflow [S0]. We do not carry that artefact into the forecast; the forecast sets working capital at the ratio the latest balance sheet actually shows, not at the FY2025 year-end ratio, so the FY2025A FCFF line should not be read as the cash the hotels produced [S0]. The problem is the stock: IDR309.5bn of debt against IDR37.2bn of cash and IDR17.1bn of equity at the FY2025 year-end. On the pack's latest balance sheet at 30 September 2026 the trend is mixed, not uniformly better: debt is lower than that year-end figure and equity is higher, but cash is slightly lower than the IDR37.2bn held at the FY2025 year-end - about one per cent lower, so the liquidity trend is flat rather than improving - and the equity, though repaired, is still thin against a hotel asset base [S0]. That is the same balance-sheet read the investment summary carries. A company in that position has no dividend capacity, and it has none: the dividend history is empty [S0]. Working capital is negative because guests and corporate accounts prepay, which flatters the cash conversion ratio but also means the reported operating working capital ratio in the data pack is a balance-sheet artefact rather than a driver we would extrapolate [S0].

The forecast cash flow is still held back in FY2026 by a working-capital charge of IDR18.8bn as the ratio moves from the FY2025 year-end level to the latest balance-sheet level while revenue grows, which is why IDR27.9bn of free cash flow to the firm is below FY2027's IDR54.0bn; from FY2027 the working capital is at a stable share of revenue and the charge turns into a small release [S0]. Capital expenditure starts at 7.5% of revenue, the FY2025 actual, and falls to 6.0% by FY2030E so that it tracks the depreciation level instead of sitting below it: a hotel that spends less than it depreciates is running down the asset, and the add-back would then be double-counted in the free cash flow. We do not capitalise the hospital: it is a development commitment, not maintenance capex, and the company has not told the market what it costs [S0][S7]. Net debt is carried at the pack's latest figure and is not assumed to be refinanced [S0]. The result is a business that earns a modest return on capital and pays most of it to the bank, which is exactly what the valuation reflects.

No FY2025 statutory filing is in our archive. The historical lines come from the data pack [S0] because the exchange's own site refuses automated retrieval by design and the issuer has no filing index we could reach; the two lines that need the filing are the depreciation note and the cash-flow statement, and both are flagged above rather than papered over. That is an evidence gap in a SELL thesis, and we state it as one. Every departure of the base case from the last actual year is listed below with its source, so the reader can see which are sourced and which are assumptions.

The base inputs differ from the FY2025 actuals as follows. Revenue growth of 47.5% applies the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the prior year's Q4/Q3 seasonal ratio to a FY2025 base that grew -38.4% [S0]. The gross margin of 54.6% is the four quarters to June 2026 with the trough quarter treated as the outlier, against a FY2025 gross margin of 43.6% [S0]. The operating cost line is 25.6% of revenue, the same four quarters' observed cost ratio, against IDR37.2bn of operating cost in FY2025 [S0]. Depreciation is IDR15.1bn in FY2026E against a reported IDR0.0bn, on the thirty-year hotel-life basis set out above because the LK note is not archived [S0][S9]. Capex is 7.5% of revenue, the FY2025 actual of IDR10.6bn, gliding down to match the depreciation charge [S0]. The tax rate is the statutory rate applied on a profitable base: FY2025 was profitable - profit before tax of IDR7.0bn and tax of IDR2.3bn, an effective rate well above statutory on a small base - and the 22.0% input follows the four quarters to June 2026, whose effective rates run between roughly twenty-two and twenty-four per cent, rather than the FY2025 statutory-plus-non-deductible mix [S0]. The output leaves the forecast about a percentage point below that 2026 run-rate, which is the one disclosed gap on this line. Working capital is carried at minus a tenth of revenue against IDR-65.1bn in FY2025, because the year-end balance is non-trade in substance rather than trading working capital [S0]. Interest is charged on the opening debt at the contractual rate, against IDR17.3bn in FY2025, with a higher FY2026 opening balance and the marginal rate reserved for the bear case [S0].

Earnings quality is poor on three of the screens we run before committing estimates. The accruals ratio is not meaningful in the usual form because the company's profit is small relative to a large, slow asset base, but the direction is clear: operating cash flow exceeds attributable profit in all three years of the record, the FY2025 trough included, which is the one favourable sign [S0]. Revenue and receivables do not diverge in a way that suggests channel stuffing, and inventory is immaterial for a hotel [S0]. The flags that matter are structural: the company sits on the high-shareholding- concentration list at 99.89% concentration, its shares have been suspended for unusual price movement and it was asked for an incidental public expose, and it has never paid a dividend [S2][S8][S0]. Under the house screen these are optics-class flags, not manipulation-class: the card reserves manipulation-class for fabricated cash or fictitious revenue, and we found neither. The HSC status and the suspension history are disclosed, explained as a cooling-down measure after a price run, and they make the price unreliable rather than the accounts false [S2][S8]. That is the same classification the governance section carries, and the consequence for the valuation is identical: a price set by the register rather than by the cash flows cannot be underwritten from the financials.

We value CLAY as a hotel owner-operator with a balance sheet, using a discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method and two market multiples as cross-checks. The method set is the industry default: sixty per cent DCF, a quarter EV/EBITDA and the rest P/E [S0]. It fits because the assets are long-lived, the cash flows are rent-like once the hotels are stabilised, and the company's main value driver is the property rather than a growth franchise. A sum-of-the-parts approach would be the alternative, but the record does not contain an independent valuation of either property, so we would be marking the buildings at our own assumption.

The discount rate is built, not chosen, and the full bridge is printed because a cost of equity that cannot be reproduced from its inputs is not a build. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5% and the levered beta 0.92, gives a higher unadjusted cost of equity before the engine deducts a default spread of 1.6%; that deduction is what brings the cost of equity to 12.0% [S0]. The spread exists because the beta is measured on a thinly traded, concentrated stock and the country premium and the distress risk are otherwise counted twice; the unlevered beta is 0.90 and the debt-to-equity ratio used to re-lever it is 0.03. That ratio is the industry target the engine applies, not CLAY's own book ratio: on the book the company is almost all liabilities, with IDR309.5bn of borrowings against IDR17.1bn of equity at FY2025 [S0], which is a ratio built on accumulated losses and describes the lender's claim on the assets rather than the market's capital structure. Using it as the weight would turn the discount rate into a cost of debt and would value the equity at a rate nobody would apply to a going concern; we keep the industry target, and we note the direction of the error rather than hide it - a book-weighted rate would be higher and the DCF lower still. With the cost of debt at 9.4% pre-tax and those weights, equity-weighted 96.7% and debt-weighted 3.3%, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.9% [S0]. The cost of debt in the WACC is the marginal 9.4%, not the 5.2% the forecast charges on the existing facilities; the difference is the refinancing risk, and it belongs there, because the WACC prices new money while the forecast pays the rate the company actually pays. That sits inside the house band for rupiah names, and we do not adjust it for the governance flags: the flags are handled in the lens and in the scenario probabilities, not by adding an arbitrary premium to the discount rate.

On those inputs the DCF gives an enterprise value of IDR642.3bn and an equity value of Rp172 a share, with the terminal value 45.9% of the total [S0]. The terminal share is moderate for a hotel with a long-lived asset base, and the terminal growth of 3.0% is below long-run nominal GDP. The cash flows are shown in the table below.

The property is the second anchor, and it is a consistency check rather than a separate valuation. The DCF's enterprise value of IDR642.3bn is of the same order as the net book value of the fixed assets, IDR428.2bn, which carries the Legian land and building and the Jakarta hotel at depreciated cost [S0][S9/F14][S9/F15]. That matters for the downside: if the cash flows disappointed permanently, the asset backing would be within a modest range of where the DCF already sits, so property value neither rescues the fundamental case nor breaks it. We looked for a Legian land transaction benchmark and for a replacement cost per square metre that we could archive and found none that met the evidence standard, so we do not mark the land up to a guess. The hospital is the one asset we value at zero, and that is an evidence statement, not a judgement: the company has disclosed no cost, funding or bed count, so there is no sunk capex figure to put in the bridge, and the development is carried as a risk to the equity rather than as an asset [S7].

The multiple cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. The peer-median EV/EBITDA of 6.5 times, applied to the pack's last-twelve-month EBITDA from Q4 2025 through Q3 2026, gives Rp97 a share, below the DCF [S0]. Two things explain the gap and neither is a depressed metric. First, the pack's last-twelve-month EBITDA is struck with a D&A charge of almost nothing, so it is effectively the EBIT line rather than an EBITDA; on our restated depreciation the same multiple would lift this leg toward the DCF, and we disclose that rather than correct it inside the engine, because the multiple belongs to quoted peers whose own EBITDA is computed by their own filings. Second, the multiple lifts the enterprise value while the net-debt bridge takes about half of it back, and the peers' 6.5 times is a multiple on their own current earnings, not on our recovery. Mechanically the model applies 6.5 times to that last-twelve-month EBITDA, subtracts the net debt of the pack's latest balance sheet and divides by the 2,570m shares, and that subtraction is what puts the value below the DCF even though the multiple looks generous. Applied to our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR75.8bn, the same multiple would raise the cross-check but still leave it below the DCF. The P/E cross-check at 15.0 times last-twelve-month earnings gives Rp215 a share, which is well above the DCF, and the engine flags the size of that gap [S0]. We do not smooth it away. A 15.0 times multiple implies a growth path the discounted cash flow does not carry: valued at the cost of equity with no growth, the same earnings are worth far less than that multiple, so the peer median is pricing either growth, or asset value, that these two hotels do not earn. It is a real market reading - it is how the market capitalises a small Indonesian hotel's reported profit - but it is the cross-check that flatters the equity, and it carries the smallest weight for that reason [S0]. The two multiples therefore bracket the DCF, the enterprise-value multiple below it and the earnings multiple above it, and the weighted value the engine carries (Rp160) sits between them. The peer set is the data pack's quoted Indonesian hotel and leisure list: twelve names carry an earnings multiple and eleven an EV/EBITDA, and the earnings median of 15.0 times is struck on all twelve [S0]. Bukit Uluwatu Villa, the desk's other Bali luxury name, is in that set at a multiple near eighty times, the second highest behind a name above ninety times, and we say so plainly rather than describe the peer list as one it is not [S0]. The outlier does not flatter the multiple in the way a reader might assume: with twelve observations the median sits between the seventh and the eighth, so removing one of the two highest names would move the median down to the seventh observation, about eleven times, and cut the P/E leg by more than a quarter rather than raise it [S0]. We therefore keep the set as computed and print the sensitivity instead of adjusting it by hand in either direction; adding a house estimate for Bukit Uluwatu on top of a median of quoted peers would make the multiple ours, and dropping it would make the multiple ours in the other direction. The table below renders from the engine and states what each method applies its multiple to.

The weight of the evidence is that the equity is worth a small fraction of the price. Our probability-weighted fundamental value is Rp128 a share twelve months out and Rp114 today, both after the liquidity discount, against a price of Rp2,940 [S0]. That is the answer to the valuation question, and it does not depend on the governance view: even if the hotels were managed perfectly, the enterprise value the cash flows support is a fraction of the market capitalisation.

The price itself is the second question, and here the house lens applies because CLAY is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which makes it a konglo name for our purposes [S2][S12]. The lens works in three steps. It measures the ratio of price to fundamental value, which is 25.8 times [S0]. It assumes that a share of the log gap closes over twelve months, set by the name's regime flags: 35.0% in the base regime, with the HSC status adding to the closing share [S0]. It then multiplies the twelve-month fundamental value, not today's, by the premium that survives, which gives the target of Rp1,739 [S0]. The compress parameters are shares of the log gap, so a negative one is a re-expansion, and the bull regime's is negative: in ratio terms the bull does not widen the premium slightly, it multiplies the premium ratio by itself raised to the bull power, which is a large increase in the multiple the target keeps. In the bear regime, where the gap closes by 75.0%, the target is Rp288; in the base regime it is Rp1,056; in the bull regime it is Rp4,558 [S0]. Most of the probability-weighted premium the target keeps therefore comes from the regime that assumes the gap widens, which is why the target is a statement about flows and float, not a claim that the company is worth the price.

Two fundamental values appear in this section and they are on the same basis, one year apart, not on different bases. Both are after the liquidity discount of 30.0%. The twelve-month fundamental value is Rp128 a share: the probability-weighted value of the business one year from today, which is the number the lens multiplies by the premium that survives. The today value is Rp114 a share: the same twelve-month estimate discounted back one year at the cost of equity of 12.0%, which is the number the premium ratio divides the price by. So 25.8 times is Rp2,940 divided by Rp114; it is not measured on a pre-discount base and it is not measured on the twelve-month value either. The arithmetic of the target can be rebuilt from the table: each regime prints its probability, the share of the log gap it closes, the premium it keeps and its target, so the probability-weighted premium kept times Rp128 gives Rp1,739. The HSC flag is the only adjustment the registry loads on this name today - the free float of 18.6% is above the minimum, so no free-float deadline applies, and there is no enforcement or index deletion on record [S0][S12][S13].

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF solves for the growth the market is paying for, and the answer is that FY2027E revenue growth has to be 41.5% against our 8.0% base rate - 33.5% above it - with the same margin, capex and discount rate [S0]. No plausible reading of two hotels with a fixed room count and falling arrivals gets there [S10]. The honest conclusion is that the price is not a forecast of the business at all; it is a function of the share register, and the only question for a public-market investor is whether the register changes within the horizon. That is why the target is the lens output and the rating is SELL rather than a valuation gap dressed as a recommendation.

The downside risks are concentrated in three places: the balance sheet, the destination and the regime. On the balance sheet, IDR309.5bn of debt against IDR17.1bn of equity at the FY2025 year-end, with the pack's September 2026 balance sheet showing lower debt and higher equity but still a thin cushion [S0], means a refinancing at a higher rate, or a covenant test that forces a rights issue, is a transfer of value from shareholders to lenders. The probability is moderate and the impact is high, because the equity is the thin slice. How we treat it in the model matters for reading the scenarios: the free cash flow is struck before interest and discounted at the weighted average cost of capital, so a higher rate moves the earnings and the return on equity, and only an actual share issue moves the per-share value. We do not shock a rights issue because neither its size nor its price is disclosed [S0]; it is a live risk, described here, that the valuation does not contain. On the destination, the change in foreign arrivals to Bali was -1.6% in the first eight months of 2026 and the second half of the year carries the high season; a weak high season would break the revenue recovery our base case assumes [S10]. The probability is moderate and the impact is moderate.

The governance and regime risks are harder to quantify and more important to the price. The stock has been suspended for unusual price movement and the exchange asked for an incidental public expose as a cooling-down measure [S8]. It is on the HSC list, and HSC names left the IHSG calculation on early November 2026, which removes the index demand a stock like this was priced on [S12]. The free float is 18.6%, above the fifteen per cent minimum the exchange now requires, so the transition deadline that applies to names in the twelve-and-a-half to fifteen per cent band does not bite today; the float risk here is the opposite one, a discounted rights issue that would lift the float per cent while cutting the value of each share [S13]. The MSCI consultation on Indonesia's classification, opened in October 2026 with feedback due by the end of April 2027 and a decision by the end of June, is a sector-wide event, but for a name like this it is the difference between a stock with index demand and one without [S14]. We treat these as regime risks, not as business risks, and they are why the scenario probabilities are not symmetric.

The operating risks are ordinary: a fire or closure at the Bali property would remove the larger half of revenue; the hospital project could absorb cash the hotels need; key-person risk sits with a small board. The financial risks are the ones a reader should watch: interest cover, the current portion of debt, and any sign of a rights issue. The record does not contain a maturity schedule, so we cannot date the refinancing risk; that is an evidence gap we flag rather than guess.

Our business scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers, each shocked by an equal and opposite amount. The base case assumes the FY2026 recovery holds, revenue grows 47.5% and then fades, and margins settle at the run-rate. The bear case cuts revenue growth by six points in every year, gross margin by two and raises the cost ratio by two, so the first-half recovery is the whole recovery, FY2027 growth is about two per cent and later years go flat to negative: that is a demand shock plus a cost shock of the kind FY2025 already demonstrated [S0]. It also reprices its debt: the bear pays a higher rate on the same balance and the bull a lower one, mirrored around the 5.2% the company actually paid in FY2025 rather than around a premium we assumed [S0]. That shock moves the interest line, the profit and the return on equity; it does not move the free cash flow the valuation discounts, because the free cash flow is struck before interest. The bear's value therefore comes from its three demand and margin shocks, and the rate step is a statement about the earnings and about how close a discounted rights issue is, not a second valuation shock. The rights issue itself would dilute, and that is the balance-sheet risk the model does not carry because the company has disclosed no size, price or timing [S0]. The probabilities are fifty per cent base, thirty per cent bear and twenty per cent bull: the bear is weighted above the bull because the balance sheet is thin, the destination is contracting and the regime is tightening, and that asymmetry is a sourced judgement rather than a cautious default [S10][S12]. Even the bull case does not reach the current price on fundamentals; it reaches it only through the lens, which is the point.

The regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios and are computed by the lens. In the base regime 35.0% of the gap closes, in the bear regime 75.0% closes as the regime's own bear share and the HSC adjustment compound, and in the bull regime the log gap re-expands by a tenth, which in ratio terms multiplies the premium rather than holding it, because a small float and a controller with no need to sell can sustain a price that fundamentals do not [S0]. The signposts that would change our view are specific: a material related-party transaction that moves cash out of the listed entity, a rights issue at a discount, a change in the HSC list, a suspension that lasts more than a few days, or a sustained recovery in Bali arrivals above the prior year [S12][S8][S10]. None of them is in the record today.

Ownership and control dominate this section. The company is a subsidiary of PT Citra Putra Mandiri and part of OSO Group, and the two hotels are presented as group assets [S0][S7]. The share register is among the most concentrated on the exchange. Two different measures are often confused and both are true here. The exchange's HSC test is the cumulative holding of the ten largest shareholders, scripless plus scrip, and it is that measure that stands at 99.89% for CLAY, which is why the name is on the list at all [S2]. The free float - shares outside the controlling and five-per-cent-plus holders - is 18.6% in the data pack's market block, which takes the field from the exchange's IDX-IC free-float registry [S0]; the market-wide free-float release does not list CLAY by name, so that registry field is the best evidence we have and we label it as such. The two measures are consistent: a controller and a handful of minority holders individually below five per cent can add up to the HSC threshold while leaving a float of that size. On the float measure the name is above the fifteen per cent minimum the exchange now requires, so the 2027 transition deadline that applies to names below it does not bite today [S13]; the data pack's insider share of almost the whole company reflects the HSC measure, not the float [S0]. We could not archive the annual report that names the ultimate beneficiary, the shareholders above five per cent and any pledged shares; that is a gap in our evidence, and we say so rather than fill it from press summaries.

Related-party exposure is the channel to watch. The company operates inside a group that owns the brand and the parent, and the public expose describes the business as sitting under the group rather than as an independent operator [S7]. The record does not quantify related-party revenue, purchases or loans, so we cannot put a percentage on it; we can say that the structure makes it the most likely route by which value leaves the listed entity, and that the hospital project is the obvious candidate for a related-party construction or land transaction [S7]. The equity screen treats unquantified related-party gravity as a flag, not a finding.

The dividend record is empty: no dividend in the price history, and the company has been loss-making or barely profitable for most of its listed life [S0]. That is defensible for a company with this balance sheet, but it also means the shareholder return is entirely a price return, which for a stock at this multiple is a bet on the register rather than on the business. Capital allocation has been defensive: the FY2025 cost cut preserved operating profit, and capex has been minimal apart from the recent year's spend [S0]. The hospital is the first genuine growth allocation, and it is being made without disclosed numbers.

The board is small and the disclosures are thin. The data pack lists a president director, a finance director and a company secretary, and the public expose was led by the president director and the finance director [S0][S7]. We have no auditor opinion in the archive, no audit-committee report and no board-independence data; the annual report would carry them and it is not in our record. On the IDX regime screens, the HSC listing and the suspension history are the two flags that matter, and both are disclosed rather than hidden [S2][S8]. Our classification is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: we found no fabricated cash, no fictitious revenue and no restatement in the record, but the concentration and the suspension mean the price should be treated as unreliable until the exchange's concerns are resolved.

ESG exposure is modest and mostly asset-level. Neither property publishes environmental data and the group does not report a sustainability policy in our archive [S7]. The Bali property is a large building on a 22,850 square metre site in a water-stressed destination, so water use, waste and local employment are the material issues; the Jakarta hotel is a city building with ordinary energy and labour exposure. The company does not publish a sustainability report in our archive, so we cannot score it. The social dimension of the hospital is positive if it is built, and the governance dimension is the one that dominates: a small board, a concentrated register and a controlling group are the ESG facts an investor is actually underwriting here.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The FY2026 audited results are the first full-year test of the recovery, and the company's own plan puts the hospital completion in the 2027 window [S7]. The regime calendar is as important: the free-float transition deadline, the MSCI consultation deadline and decision, and the quarterly HSC review all fall inside the next twelve months [S13][S14][S12]. Any of them can move the price without moving the business, although the free-float deadline does not bind CLAY at the current float.

The KPIs we will monitor are the ones the company actually discloses. Monthly or quarterly Bali arrival data from BPS is the leading indicator for The Stones [S10]. The company's own revenue line and its cost ratio are the two numbers that decide whether the recovery is real; we will compare each interim against our IDR209.4bn forecast [S0]. Interest expense and the debt balance are the balance-sheet KPIs, and any announcement of a rights issue, a related-party transaction or a new suspension is a governance KPI that would change the rating before it changes the model.

What would make us wrong is worth stating plainly [S0]. A sustained recovery in arrivals, a refinancing that lowers the interest burden, and a hospital project that is funded outside the listed entity would all raise the fundamental value, and a re-rating of small Indonesian hotel stocks would compress the premium without any change at the company. Our fundamental value is not a floor on the share price; it is an estimate of what the cash flows are worth, and the market has shown that it can price this register far above that for a long time. The rating is a statement about the expected twelve-month return under the house lens, and the reader should treat the lens, not the DCF, as the part of the target that could move fastest.

bear.narrative: The first-half recovery is real but it is all there is: the Legian high season disappoints because foreign arrivals to Bali were already falling in the year to August 2026 [S10], the Jakarta corporate segment does not recover, and revenue growth runs six points below base in every year, so FY2027 is about 2% and later years go flat to negative. Gross margin is two points lower as the mix and the fixed cost of sales bite, and SG&A two points higher. The thin equity - Rp17.1bn against Rp428bn of fixed assets at FY2025 [S0] - also means the debt is repriced up by 0.8pp from the 5.2% actually paid [S0]. That fourth shock moves interest expense, net profit and ROE, not the free cash flow to the firm, which is struck before interest: the bear's valuation effect comes from the three demand and margin shocks, and the rate step is what a refinancing would do to the earnings and to the case for a discounted rights issue, which we describe but do not shock (no size, price or timing disclosed). All four shocks are mirrored with the bull; the bear is weighted above the bull on the arrival and balance-sheet evidence, not on the rate step [S10][S0].

bull.narrative: Arrivals stabilise, the Legian hotel's rate recovery holds through the 2026-27 high seasons and the Menteng hotel benefits from a Jakarta corporate and MICE recovery, so revenue growth runs six points above base with gross margin two points higher and SG&A two points lower as the fixed cost base is absorbed. Mirrored with the bear on the same three demand and margin drivers; no unsourced re-rating and no share issuance. On the debt side the rate falls 0.8pp below the 5.2% actually paid, the exact mirror of the bear's reset [S0]. The rate shock is an earnings and ROE effect in both cases, not a valuation input, because the free cash flow to the firm is struck before interest.

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is built from the nine-month actual, not from a growth rate applied to FY2025: the pack's 2026Q1-Q3 revenue is Rp156.12bn and the fourth quarter is set at the prior year's own Q4/Q3 seasonal ratio (2025Q4 Rp38.45bn over 2025Q3 Rp50.45bn, 0.762) applied to 2026Q3's Rp69.97bn, i.e. Rp53.3bn, which also means Q4 grows at Q3's year-on-year rate of +38.7% rather than collapsing [S0]. That gives FY2026E revenue of Rp209.4bn, +47.5% on FY2025, against the pack's LTM revenue of Rp194.6bn and below the FY2023-FY2024 level of Rp224.6-230.6bn, so the year is a recovery to, not above, the pre-trough business [S0]. FY2027-30 then fade to 8/6/5/4% as the recovery laps a destination whose foreign arrivals fell 1.62% in the year to August 2026, and terminal growth is 3% [S10].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2024 gross margin was 51.9% and the four quarters to June 2026 (2025Q3-2026Q2) run 54.6%, against 43.6% in the FY2025 trough year when revenue fell a third against a partly fixed cost of sales [S0]. We hold the four-quarter 54.6%, not a rounded-down 50%: the trough ratio is the outlier, the pre-trough level and the run-rate agree on a margin in the low-to-mid fifties, and the twelve months to September 2026 print a higher gross margin still, so the calibration sits inside the observed run-rate rather than above it [S0]. We have no archived segment-margin evidence of a permanent mix shift toward lower-margin F&B, so a haircut below the run-rate would be unsourced caution.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The template's EBIT is gross profit less SG&A with D&A carried separately, so SG&A must be the all-in cost line the LK reports (26.2% of FY2025 revenue). On the four quarters to June 2026 the pack gives a 54.6% gross margin and a 25.6% cost ratio, i.e. a 29.0% EBIT margin [S0]. We hold that decomposition rather than a rounded 21% cost ratio, which was an arithmetic error: 54.6 less 25.6 is the 29.0% EBIT margin the same four quarters show, and the twelve months to September 2026 run a higher cost ratio and a higher EBIT margin at once, so 25.6% and 29.0% sit inside, not above, the observed range [S0]. That gives an EBIT margin of 29.0% against 17.4% in FY2025: the step is the revenue recovery against a cost base already cut, not a new margin assumption.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue (a LEVEL held near Rp15bn, expressed as a ratio)
assumptions.basis: The data pack reports D&A of Rp0.01bn against PP&E of Rp428bn, which cannot be the real charge [S0]. The charge is a LEVEL, not a share of revenue: a building stock of that size depreciated over a thirty-year hotel life is roughly Rp14-16bn a year, and the FY2025 LK depreciation note is not in the archive, so the level is the assumption. The template applies da_pct to revenue, so the values below fall as revenue grows and hold the charge at about Rp15bn a year through FY2030E (Rp15.1bn in FY2026E on the higher revenue base), reaching the terminal ratio from FY2031E. Holding a constant share of revenue instead would make the add-back rise on a shrinking asset base and inflate the DCF.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was Rp10.6bn, 7.5% of revenue, and FY2024 Rp3.4bn; the two hotels are built and the spend is maintenance and room refurbishment [S0]. We start at the last actual 7.5% and let the ratio fall as revenue grows so that capex tracks the D&A level (about Rp14-15bn a year) rather than sitting below it, which would shrink the asset base while the add-back rose. The ratio therefore reaches 6.0% by FY2030E and 5.5% in the long run, equal to the terminal D&A ratio so that net investment is zero at terminal growth. The Royal Sukadana hospital is treated as a separate development risk: the company has disclosed no cost or funding for it [S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The pack's FY2025 year-end ratio of -45.8% is driven by large non-trade balances (advance deposits, related-party and tax items) and by the debt reclassification, not by trading working capital [S0]. The latest balance sheet already shows the normalisation: reported operating working capital was -Rp43.05bn at 30 September 2026 on LTM revenue of Rp194.57bn, i.e. -22.1% [S0]. We set the forecast ratio to that latest actual rather than to the FY2025 year-end, because the adjustment has already happened inside the 2026 actuals and modelling it a second time would charge an outflow the reported balance sheet no longer supports; a hotel runs a small negative working capital because guests prepay.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory corporate rate of 22% applied on a profitable base. FY2025 was profitable - PBT Rp7.02bn, tax Rp2.32bn, a 33.0% effective rate - so the FY2025 rate is not a loss-year artefact; it reflects non-deductible items on a small profit [S0]. FY2023 and FY2024 paid 55.5% and 53.9% [S0]. The 22% input is set from the four quarters to June 2026, whose effective rates run 24.2%, 22.5% and 23.6%, i.e. close to statutory. The forecast therefore sits about 1pp below that 2026 run-rate, the disclosed gap.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The rate the company actually paid: FY2025 interest expense of Rp17.34bn on average debt of about Rp332bn is 5.2%, which is the last actual and therefore the base case [S0]. We hold it rather than charging the 9.5% marginal rate the WACC uses, because the marginal rate prices new money and the record shows what the existing facilities cost [S0]. Two consequences we state in the report: this line flows into interest expense, net profit and ROE, NOT into the free cash flow to the firm, which is struck before interest (so it does not enter the DCF); and the scenario shocks are mirrored at 0.8pp around this actual rather than around an assumed premium.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default, average of FY2023A, FY2024A and FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1])); cash balances earn a negligible deposit rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No refinancing is sourced; we hold debt flat and let the cash flow pay it down through the net-debt bridge rather than assume new facilities [S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; no recurring non-operating income is sourced

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities are immaterial (Rp0.07bn of balance-sheet minority at FY2025) and the quarterly minority line is near zero [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company has never paid a dividend in the price history and told the market in 2019 that it would not distribute while loss-making [S0][S5]. Equity of Rp17bn against Rp428bn of fixed assets leaves no distributable reserve, so payout is zero through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No completed issuance is in the archived record; the reported 2,570m shares have been stable since the 2019 IPO of 520m shares [S0][S3]. Dilution is a judgement, not a reported event: no archived source states that a rights issue is planned or under discussion, and we would be inventing a term sheet to model one. With debt of Rp256.29bn against equity of Rp45.44bn at 30 September 2026 [S0], a discounted issue is nonetheless the obvious funding route for the hospital, so the risk is described in the report and carries zero weight in the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR, below long-run nominal GDP; a two-hotel Jakarta/Bali operator with no pipeline beyond an unfunded hospital should not carry more [S7].

challenges.challenge: da_pct is 9% of revenue in every year (fund record:67-83), yet its stated basis derives a LEVEL: PP&E 428.2bn / 30 years = 14.3bn ('roughly Rp14-16bn a year'). The engine applies it to revenue, so D&A grows to Rp24.5bn by FY2035E (explain --line da) while capex is only 5% of revenue, 9.4bn rising to 13.6bn (explain --line capex) and PP&E must shrink: depreciation cannot rise 70% on a declining asset base. Because FCFF = ebit*(1-tax) + da - capex - delta_nwc (explain --line fcff), the excess add-back is worth roughly Rp78bn of EV, about Rp30/share or 23% of the DCF's Rp131, and fund record:253 tells the reader 'EBIT and cash flow are unaffected by that choice'. The pack's own LTM D&A is Rp4.9bn and FY2025A D&A is Rp0.01bn, so nothing in the archive supports a revenue-scaled charge.
challenges.answer: D&A is now a level, not a share: da_pct falls from 0.080 in FY2026E to 0.064 by FY2030E so the charge holds near Rp15bn (PP&E Rp428bn over a 30-year hotel life), and capex starts at the FY2025 actual 7.5% and glides to 5.5% so it tracks D&A instead of sitting below it. The 'cash flow unaffected' sentence is deleted and section 3 now says EBIT is unaffected but the add-back and FCFF depend on the level. The DCF fell from Rp131 to Rp124 a share and the 60/25/15 blend re-ran [S0][S9].

challenges.challenge: The calibration BLOCK (FY2026E EBITDA margin +15.6pp vs FY2025A) is answered by saying the step is 'mostly the missing depreciation being restored' (packet QC justification). At a consistent 9% D&A convention FY2025A margin is 26.4%, not the 17.4% the gate compares, so about +6.6pp of genuine margin expansion on 32% revenue growth is passed off as an accounting restoration. The pack's LTM D&A is 4.9bn (2.8% of revenue), not 9%, so the restoration is small.
challenges.answer: The calibration is now answered on the comparable line, EBIT margin, not on the pack's zero-D&A EBITDA: 17.4% to 28.0% on 32% revenue growth, and the mechanism is sourced - the FY2025 cost line was cut from Rp70.6bn to Rp37.2bn while EBIT held, and the four quarters to June 2026 already run a 29% EBIT margin. The old 'missing depreciation restored' justification is deleted [S0].

challenges.challenge: fund record:321 claims that applying the 6.9x peer multiple to FY2026E EBITDA 'would produce a value above the DCF'. It does not: 6.9 x 61.87 = EV 427, less the 223.5 bridge = equity 203.4, or Rp79/share against the DCF's Rp131. Nor is the LTM metric behind the Rp62 a 'depressed' one: LTM EBITDA is 55.7bn at a 31.8% margin versus FY2025A's 17.4% (datapack ltm). The -52% cross-check divergence flagged by the model is therefore dismissed on a false statement rather than explained.
challenges.answer: The false claim is gone. The report now says applying 6.9x to FY2026E EBITDA raises the cross-check but still leaves it below the DCF because the net-debt bridge takes about half the enterprise value, states that the LTM metric is the strongest four quarters rather than a depressed one, and adds a table naming the metric behind each multiple [S0].

challenges.challenge: The report asserts both a 99.89% concentration (F11, S2 quote 'CLAY: PT Citra Putra Realty Tbk (99,890%, -)') and an 18.6% free float (§6 and the investment summary). Both cannot describe the same register. The 18.6% has no archived source in the company folder - model.konglo.profile.free_float cites deck source S25 - and §5 uses it to call the name compliant with the 15% minimum. If the BEI concentration figure is right the float is about 0.1%, the company is in breach, and the lens's ff_deadline adjustment (+0.05, left unapplied) should bite.
